sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section discusses the peculiar arrangement of the discourses for the month of Elul in Likkutei Torah, questioning why they were included in the section of Re'eh and not in Shoftim, and notes the significance of the discourse beginning on page 32 (Lamed-Beis), which is the heart of the book.

translations.translation: Now, in the totality of the discourses of the month of Elul in Likkutei Torah,
which were arranged and printed by the Tzemach Tzedek,
we find a remarkable thing,
that in these discourses he did not repeat at all
(a heading)
as a separate [section]
"Discourses for Elul",
and they were included in the discourses for Parshas Re'eh.
And an explanation is needed for the connection of the discourses of Elul with Parshas Re'eh.
And also it is necessary to understand why discourses for Parshas Shoftim were not printed in Likkutei Torah.
Although there are many discourses from the Alter Rebbe on Parshas Shoftim,
both on the beginning of the portion
(Shoftim and Shotrim)
and on verses in the middle of the portion.
And as is also printed in Ohr HaTorah of the Tzemach Tzedek,
and likewise in the discourses of the Mitteler Rebbe,
that several of both of them are founded on the discourses of the Alter Rebbe,
and discourses were printed for Parshas Re'eh
(which is before Parshas Shoftim)
and Parshas Teitzei
(which is after it)
and discourses for Parshas Shoftim were not printed
(and behold, the discourses of Elul are connected
(also)
to Parshas Shoftim).
Also it is necessary to understand that the fixed time of Rosh Chodesh Elul in Parshas Shoftim compels that there is a connection between them, and what it is.
And to note a remarkable matter in the aforementioned discourse
(beginning "Ani L'Dodi")
in Likkutei Torah,
which begins and is printed on page 32 (Lamed-Beis).
And it can be said that in any case, the number 32 (Lamed-Beis) has a special content,
as discussed elsewhere
a hint of the matter that in chapter 32
of Tanya, the matter of "Love your fellow as yourself" is explained,
because the matter of love of Israel is the heart and the main principle,
as our sages said,
"This is a great principle in the Torah."
And likewise it can be said regarding page 32 (Lamed-Beis) of the book Mishneh Torah in Likkutei Torah, which was arranged for print by the Tzemach Tzedek,
and that is,
that on this page
(in this discourse)
is the heart of Likkutei Torah on Mishneh Torah.
And even if you say that this discourse being printed on page 32 (Lamed-Beis) was later,
nevertheless, it is close to say,
that since this is a book of Torah,
and particularly according to the well-known teaching of the Baal Shem Tov,
it is possible to learn a lesson in the service of man even from such details.

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section explains the connection between the Elul discourses and the concept of "heart" (page 32), based on the analogy of the king in the field, where all are equal and barriers are nullified, reflecting the mutual heart-relationship between Israel and G-d, and linking this to Parshas Re'eh's theme of face-to-face revelation.

translations.translation: And the explanation of all this can be said,
based on what was explained earlier, that the point of the aforementioned discourse is that the service of the month of Elul is like the parable of the king in the field.
And based on this, the connection of the discourses of Elul with
(page)
32 (Lamed-Beis) will be sweetened,
for when the king is in the field,
behold, "the field" equalizes all who are found in it,
since there, each one
(without distinction)
is permitted and able to greet him,
and he receives them all, etc.
(unlike when he is in his capital city,
and especially in his palace,
where only the elite and select individuals enter to the king).
And furthermore,
when the king is in the field,
then the partitions etc. between the king and the people are nullified,
and he receives them all with a pleasant countenance and shows them a smiling face.
And in general
(and particularly in Elul),
"Ani"
(Israel)
"v'Dodi"
(the Holy One, blessed be He),
each one of them is, as it were, a heart for the other.
And this depends on the unity of Israel
("Ani")
(that when the king is in the field, all are equal),
as explained in Igeres HaKodesh.
And it can be said that this is also the connection with Parshas Re'eh,
the matter of "seeing" (Re'eh),
the illumination of the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy is that it should be face to face,
the innerness of His will, blessed be He, to Israel and the innerness of the will of Israel to Him, blessed be He
(similar to the above that each one of them is a heart for the other).
And as it is written, "See, I am giving before you,"
the aspect of face to face.
[However, the matter of "Shoftim and Shotrim," etc.
is, on the contrary,
the opposite of equality,
to clarify the distinction
(and the partitions)
between one another,
between one law and another, etc.]

sections.sectionSummaryBrief: This section elaborates on the superiority of the "field" over the "desert" and the "city," explaining that the field represents the work of refining and elevating worldly matters into holiness, akin to the concept of bread which sustains the heart and contains a Divine spark.

translations.translation: And now, it is explained in the continuation of the discourse there,
that just as there is an aspect of field, so too there is an aspect of desert,
"a land not sown"
"where no man dwells."
And in the parable of the month of Elul, the king is in the field
(and not in the desert)
for the field is superior to the desert.
And also simply, the desert is a land not sown,
unlike the field, which is a place of sowing and growth of bread,
"a land
from which bread comes forth."
For the bread is refined and elevated,
and "bread sustains the heart of man,"
for "not on bread alone does man live, but on every utterance of the mouth of Hashem"
that is in the bread,
the G-dly spark within the bread
(as explained in the writings of the Arizal
and in many places).
And it follows that the novelty of the field over the city and desert is,
that the city consists of houses within the boundary of holiness,
and the desert is outside the boundary of holiness
("where no man dwells"),
and the content of the field is the refinement of matters that are outside the house and their entry into holiness.
And this is the entirety of man's service,
to refine the matters of the world and elevate them to G-dliness.
And also for this reason, all the offerings are called "My offering, My bread for My fire,"
the matter of bread,
and in the language of our sages,
"My shepherdess, my sustenance."
